title: Deviated nasal septum: understanding a blocked nose
intro: The septum is the wall of cartilage and bone separating the nasal passages. It is rarely perfectly straight. A bend matters when it contributes to troublesome obstruction, rather than simply appearing on an examination. Assessment should connect the anatomy with your symptoms and check for other treatable causes before deciding about surgery.

sections.heading: What symptoms can mean
paragraphs: A narrowed passage can make breathing through the nose difficult, sometimes more on one side, with mouth breathing, dryness or disturbed sleep. A previous injury or differences during facial growth may explain the shape. However, allergy, swollen nasal lining, enlarged turbinates, polyps and other conditions can also obstruct airflow. Snoring, facial pain or tiredness alone do not prove that the septum is responsible. Breathing pauses during sleep need assessment for sleep apnoea; straightening the septum is not a guaranteed cure for that disorder. A visible bend without meaningful symptoms usually needs no treatment.

sections.heading: Prepare for an ear, nose and throat assessment
paragraphs: Describe which side feels blocked, whether it changes, how long it has lasted and effects on sleep, exercise or work. Mention injuries, nosebleeds, reduced smell, allergy symptoms, previous surgery and every nasal spray you use. The clinician examines inside and outside the nose and may use a thin viewing instrument. Additional allergy tests, airflow measurements, scans or a sleep assessment are selected according to findings, rather than being necessary for everyone. Persistent one-sided obstruction, especially with blood-stained discharge, deserves prompt medical review instead of repeated self-treatment as an ordinary cold.

sections.heading: Treat swelling without expecting medicines to straighten cartilage
paragraphs: A saline product or treatment for allergy may improve symptoms when irritation or swelling contributes. A prescribed steroid nasal spray reduces inflammation; it does not move a bent septum. Ask about technique, the trial period and when to review the result. Directing a spray toward the outer nasal wall rather than the central septum may help avoid irritation. Decongestant sprays give short relief but prolonged use can worsen blockage; follow the product's short duration limit and ask a pharmacist about suitability. Do not try to straighten the nose with fingers, tools or unproven devices.

sections.heading: Discuss what septoplasty can and cannot achieve
paragraphs: Septoplasty adjusts the internal partition to improve airflow when symptoms and examination support a structural cause. Sometimes enlarged turbinates are treated as well. Changing the external appearance requires a separate discussion about rhinoplasty or a combined operation. Ask what improvement is realistic, what non-surgical options remain and whether other causes of obstruction will still need treatment. Risks include bleeding, infection, a hole in the septum, persistent blockage and occasionally changes in shape or sensation. Anaesthetic risks and individual health also matter. In growing children, timing and need require specialist judgement. Improvement is possible, but complete or permanent relief is not guaranteed.

sections.heading: Recovery and warning signs
paragraphs: Temporary blockage and discomfort after surgery do not necessarily mean failure. Obtain written instructions about nasal care, any packing or splints, work, exercise, nose blowing and follow-up; do not remove internal supports yourself. Increasing pain or blockage, fever, foul discharge or substantial bleeding need urgent advice from the treating team. After a fresh injury, a painful swelling inside the nose may be a septal haematoma needing emergency assessment, even if the outside looks acceptable. Uncontrolled bleeding, clear watery leakage after head injury, severe headache with visual changes or serious breathing difficulty also require emergency care. These are different from a long-standing stable bend.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: two causes together
examples.text: Mira has a bent septum and seasonal sneezing. Allergy treatment reduces swelling but one side remains troublesome. She records the remaining sleep and breathing problems and discusses whether surgery could address the structural part, while continuing the appropriate allergy plan.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: an injury changes the plan
examples.text: After being hit during sport, Leo develops increasing blockage and tender swelling inside his nose. He seeks emergency assessment for a possible blood collection rather than waiting for an elective appointment about a deviated septum.

questions: Which findings explain my blockage, and are other causes present?
What improvement and risks should I expect from surgery compared with further medical treatment?
What is my recovery plan, and which changes require urgent help?
